This data screening protocol is based on the long-string data-screening method (DeSimone et al., 2015); however, this adaptation (designed for the current study; see also Brown et al., 2023) focused more on repeated implausible responses rather than all repeated responses. All questionnaire responses were mandatory to avoid missing data, participants were instructed to withdraw if they preferred not to answer items. For Sample 8, these exclusion criteria were pre-registered (https://osf.io/3je7y), with additional criteria included to reduce potential added demographic variance from the broader Prolific Academic population. This was set through the Prolific Academic in-built recruitment filters, which specified that participants had to be aged 18-35, fluent in English, and be UK-based. The recruitment filter was also set so that approximately 50% of the sample were female, 1 For reasons of transparency (i.e., to avoid the 'file drawer effect') all samples collected are noted here. However, as a power analysis revealed that the sample of 20 parent-child pairs was highly underpowered for the intended analysis of parental ratings (required N = 80), this is omitted from the main paper: The power analysis and exploratory correlations are reported in Supplementary materials 2. and 50% male. Additionally, specific criteria were also registered to counter potential automated bot-responses which are more prevalent on paid survey platforms (Xu et al., 2022): Participants had to score >95% approval ratings on previous Prolific Academic studies, they had to correctly respond to at least one of two attention checks requiring a specific pattern of response, and survey completions faster than 3SD from the mean were also excluded. Additionally, though not pre-registered, we excluded 19 participants whose Qualtrics CAPTCHA response score was below .4, suggesting non-human bot responses. Ethical approval for all studies were granted by the [REDACTED FOR MASKED REVIEW] Ethics Committee (Approved codes: [REDACTED FOR MASKED REVIEW]).

All participants completed informed consent and were debriefed.

Sample Size Determination and Power Analyses

The stopping rules for data collection of most samples were defined by the maximum number of participants who could be collected within a set timeframe or from a single recruitment event. For the pilot sample 1, and samples 5, 6 and 7, data collection was stopped after a single academic year; whilst for sample 2 due to a single academic year being insufficient to recruit a large enough sample, collection was stopped after 2 years. For samples 3 and 4, data collection was stopped after all available participants had completed the study as part of a required workshop activity. Sample 8 was collected primarily for the purposes of a separate study (separately pre-registered at http://osf.io/3hqu7), for which funding had been gained to cover the Prolific participant payments.

Our pre-registered sample size was determined by that study (including an additional 10% for exclusions, total N = 435).

However, the pre-registration for the present study included an a priori power analysis outlining the sensitivity of the planned analyses -see below for further details; https://osf.io/3je7y). Analysis of each sample did not commence until data collection had stopped. The statistical power for all reported analyses is outlined in the relevant sections immediately below. All power analyses for correlations were conducted with two-tails to provide sensitivity to detect effects in either direction with the novel measure.

Factor Analysis.

The samples in which EFA were run (i.e., Samples 2 and 3) were well powered, based on recommended guidelines based on minimum sample size (N > 300; Comrey & Lee, 1992), and minimum number of participants per item (i.e., 10:1 ratio; Osborne & Costello, 2004; Carpenter, 2018). Further, for samples where CFA was used (Samples 4, 5 and 8), a sensitivity analysis using the semPower package in R (Moshagen & Erdfelder, 2016), revealed that the final samples exceeded the minimum required N of 270 needed to detect an RMSEA of .04, for the most complex CFA model we analysed (see bi-factor model below in Table 2; degrees of freedom = 127, 19 observed variables, α = .05, 1-β = .9).

Internal Reliability Analyses.

A power analysis for Cronbach's alpha revealed that to detect a minimum acceptable level of .7, with an estimated level of .8, a sample of 162 participants was required, based on the average number of items per subscale (M = 5; Arifin, 2022; Bonett & Wright, 2015). Internal reliability was only assessed in these samples which met the required N, specifically Samples 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8.

Test-Retest.

Based on the expectation that a stable cognitive trait would produce a large effect size, we conducted a power analysis with the expected effect of r = .5 based on common statistical guidelines (Cohen, 1988). This revealed that a minimum sample of 34 participants for both T1 and T2 measures would be required (α = .05, β = .9, two-tailed). We note that this effect is in line with T1-T2 correlations between reports of ADHD (r > .6; Kessler et al., 2007; Matza et al., 2011; Silverstein et al., 2018). Our sample of 59 was therefore adequately powered to detect an effect reflecting a stable genetically determined cognitive trait.

Correlational Analysis.

The correlation analysis to assess the relationship between the OAQ and existing measures of attention and neurodivergent traits was designed to primarily detect strong relationships, indicative of either an overlapping factor or common underlying factor. The minimum requirement to detect strong relationships indicative of this pattern would be a large correlation: r = .5. All samples were adequately powered to detect a relationship of this strength, required N > 34 (α = .05, β = .9, two-tailed). Almost all samples were also powered to detect moderate sized relationships as well (r > .3), with the exception of Sample 6 which was powered to detect effects greater than r = .39 (α = .05, 1-β = .9, two-tailed).

Inattentional Blindness (IB) Task Analysis.

To achieve a large sample to identify the relationship between Observant Attention and detection of the unexpected stimulus in the IB task, we included the static IB task in Samples 2, 5, 6, and 7, and merged these as part of a large sample mega-analysis. The use of a mega-analytic approach also provides a more exact estimate of cumulative effect sizes when small samples are included, relative to a meta-analytic approach, as it factors in the known within-study variance and normality (Burke et al., 2017; Debray et al., 2013). Based on the final numbers of participants who reported missing the stimulus versus those who reported detecting the stimulus and were able to locate it (n = 274 versus 167), a sensitivity power analysis revealed we achieved power to detect a small effect of d = .24 (α = .05, 1-β = .80, One-tailed). See 'Classification of Inattentional Blindness' section below for information on awareness grouping criteria.

As mentioned above, the sample size for Sample 8 (N = 435) was determined in relation to, and hence constrained by, the requirements of a separate funded project (although the IB task was added solely for the purposes of the present study).

Taking into account unpredictable group allocations, a priori power analysis indicated that this sample size was underpowered to replicate the effect size previously found in the present investigation using the mega-analytic approach, d = .23 (required N = 496, α = .05, 1-β = .80, One-tailed, group allocation ratio = .621). However, we reasoned that, given some minor task changes designed to improve signal to noise, it was still worthwhile to provide a pre-registered test for a slightly larger effect size, comparable to previous published findings: Our pre-registration (https://osf.io/3je7y) noted that our sample was adequately powered to detect effects in the range of one of the few previous studies to demonstrate a correlation between a self-report measure (Big Five Inventory: Openness) and a static IB task (d = .259, group allocation ratio = .634; α = .05, 1-β = .80, One-tailed; Kreitz et al., 2015).

Unfortunately, fewer participants than expected met criteria for allocation to detected versus missed conditions (only 69%; see Supplementary Materials 3 for IB exclusion criteria). After applying these criteria, the final sample available for comparison was N = 294 (detected n = 126; missed n = 168). A sensitivity power analysis showed that, with these group sizes, Sample 8 was adequately powered to detect an effect of d =.29, but underpowered to detect the preregistered effect size (d = .259) or our earlier mega-analytic estimate (d = .23).

Materials

Observant Attention Questionnaire (OAQ)

Overview of Item Generation and Scale Development. The research team first generated 40 items reflecting everyday instances of experiences that could reflect either effective observation or failures of awareness (the latter to be reverse scored). These were based on the real-world experiences of team members and their acquaintances, which included people identifying as having varying levels of observant attention. Items reflecting failures of awareness were typically situations where the lapse became apparent through an immediate consequence (e.g., not noticing a traffic light turning green until prompted by another driver), social feedback (e.g., not noticing a friend had changed their clothing), or delayed awareness of a stimulus that eventually entered awareness (e.g., failing to notice knocking at the door for some time).

Initial exploratory factor analysis (EFA) in Sample 1 indicated a similar factor structure to the final OAQ, however, the original pool of items contained an imbalance in the distribution of visual versus non-visual examples across different types of observant attention, potentially causing bias in the items. To address this, the item pool was expanded in Sample 2 with additional items providing more non-visual examples of lower-salience noticing and more visual examples of salient alerting stimuli. The enlarged pool was then refined across multiple samples using recursive EFA. Specifically, first, after unconstrained EFA failed to return a clear set of factors in Sample 2, item reduction was conducted in this sample by restricting extraction to items which loaded on three fixed factors. This was informed by screeplot inspection and plausible number of relevant factors observed in Sample 1. The smaller pool of retained items that loaded clearly on these fixed factors were then analysed with unconstrained EFA in Sample 3 to identify the final set of items. Full details of the scale development procedure are provided in Supplementary Materials 4. After extraction and confirmatory analyses (see Results section below), the final version of the novel Observant Attention Questionnaire contained 19-items. Ratings were along a 7-point Likert scale, ranging from 'very atypical of me' (score 1) to 'very typical of me' (score 7), the midpoint was labelled with 'neither typical or atypical of me'. Participants were given the instruction prior to the study: "This next questionnaire involves several statements which may or may not apply to you, generally. You must rate whether the statements are VERY ATYPICAL or VERY TYPICAL of you, or somewhere in between, using a 7-point scale. Some of the questions are very similar, do not worry too much about being perfectly consistent across these questions." CFA revealed that a bi-factor model was the best fit to the data with a general Observant Attention factor containing 16-items, these items contributed to the total Observant Attention Score taken as the main outcome measure (see Results for more details). These 16 items also contributed to three subscales reflecting Noticing awareness (8 items), Alerting awareness (6 items), and Olfactory awareness (2 items). A fourth Distractibility (3 items) subscale was also measured which was not included in the Observant Attention total score, as it reflects a distinct but theoretically relevant factor (see Results for more details). Due to the different number of items within each subscale, the average response to items on a subscale, rather than total sum, was taken as the final score to facilitate interpretation.

Large Language Model (LLM) Content Validity Check.

LLMs operate by identifying and predicting linguistic patterns, based on statistical regularities within large text corpora. They can serve as an independent method for assessing whether questionnaire items are typically associated with a construct in natural language use, thus allowing us to check whether the selected items were consistent with the intended construct of Observant Attention (for related approaches see Milano et al., 2025; Poźniak et al. 2026). Given the intention to measure the construct of observant attention, as understood by the general population, two LLMs -Google's Gemini 2.5 (Google DeepMind, 2025) and Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Anthopic, 2025) models -were used to provide an additional independent test of content/face validity of the items for measuring the intended construct (i.e. Observant Attention).

To perform the LLM content validity check, the final selected set of 19 items was presented to the LLMs along with the following prompt: 'What do the following questionnaire items appear to be measuring (scores on a scale from very atypical of me to very typical of me, R indicates reverse scored items)'. (prompt entered on 13 th November 2025). To ensure the LLM content analysis check was not influenced by past researcher input, an account with no prior queries or interactions relating to the present project or research topic was used.

Both LLMs identified the primary themes of perceptual awareness and observant attention as well as a distinct subset of items reflecting attentional control, as can be seen in these opening sentences of their output (for full LLM output see Supplementary materials 5):

Gemini Output. 'Based on the items provided, this questionnaire appears to be measuring observational skills and attentional control. A person scoring highly on this scale would be described as highly observant, perceptually sensitive to their surroundings, and able to maintain focus.

Claude Output. 'Based on the questionnaire items provided, this scale appears to be measuring **perceptual awareness** or **observational attention**specifically the ability to notice and detect environmental details, changes, and sensory information across multiple modalities' ('attentional control' is later listed as one of the three core constructs, along with 'Environmental Awareness' and 'Multisensory Perceptual Sensitivity').

Attentional Control Scale (ACS; Derryberry & Reed, 2002)

The 20-item Attentional control scale reflects the ability to effectively focus attention and switch attention voluntarily. Responses were along a 4-point scale ranging from 'Almost never' to 'Always'. Reliability analysis of the items revealed good internal consistency across all samples for both total score and subscales (α > .74).

Spontaneous and Deliberate Mind-Wandering Scales (S-MW & D-MW; Carriere et al., 2013)

The S-MW and D-MW scales are two 4-item scales, measuring the frequency that participants spontaneous and deliberate mind-wander, along a 7-point scale.

Internal reliability analysis for both subscales revealed acceptable internal consistency (α > .81).

Daydreaming Frequency Questionnaire (DDFQ; Giambra, 1993)

The 12-item DDFQ responses were measured along a 5-point scale, ranging from 'never' to 'Always' or 'infrequently' to 'Many times during the day'. Reliability analysis of the items revealed good internal consistency in Sample 6 (α = .92).

Cognitive Failures Questionnaire (CFQ; Broadbent et al., 1982)

The 25-item CFQ measures the frequency of general cognitive failures, including forgetfulness, distractibility, and triggering incorrect. Responses were along a 5-point scale ranging from 'never' to 'very often'. Reliability analysis of the items revealed good internal consistency in Sample 6 (α = .87).

Dispositional Hyperfocusing Scale (D-HF; Hupfield et al., 2018)

To measure the tendency to hyperfocus, participants completed the 12-item D-HF subscale from the Hyperfocusing questionnaire. The responses were along a 6-point Likert scale relating to how often the participant entered a state of hyperfocus, ranging from 'Never' to 'Daily'. Reliability analysis of the items revealed good internal consistency within Sample 5 (α = .89).

Difficulties with Interpersonal Distancing and Awareness Scale (DIDAS; Brown & Forster, 2023)

The DIDAS is a recently developed 8-item measure designed to capture the capacity to maintain social distance and monitor inter-personal range. Each item was rated along a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 'Never' to 'Very Often'. The total scale score is computed from the average of the 8 items, though within Sample 3 the final item was omitted due to a programming error. Internal reliability analysis for both subscales revealed good internal consistency (α = .87).

Autism Quotient (AQ; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001)

The 50-item AQ scale measures responses along a 4-point scale ranging from 'definitely agree' to 'definitely disagree', with each item scored as either one or zero depending on whether it was above or below the mid-point.

The scale consists of different subscales which are all symptomatic of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), including difficulties with social skill, lower ability to switch attention from different tasks, difficulties with communication, lower imagination, and attention to detail. The total AQ score was measured in a subset of participants from Sample 5, who had completed it at another time and consented to linking their data. The data was linked after computation of the total score, preventing reliability analysis across the individual items.

Attention to detail subscale. In Sample 6 and Sample 7, instead of the full scale, participants completed the specific attention to detail subscale, which is made up of 10-items, taken from the total 50-item scale. Internal reliability analysis for both subscales revealed acceptable internal consistency (α > .69).

Childhood ADHD Symptoms Scale (Barkley & Murphy, 1998)

To measure ADHD symptoms, participants completed the 18-item Childhood ADHD Symptoms Scale which included two 9-item subscales. One subscale measures hyperactive-impulsive behaviours whilst the other subscale measured inattention. Responses were along a 4-point scale ranging from 'never or rarely' to 'Very often'. Internal reliability analysis for both subscales revealed good internal consistency (α > .83).

Glasgow Sensory Questionnaire (GSQ; Robertson & Simmons, 2013)

To measure the extreme hypo-sensitivity and hyper-sensitivity to sensory stimuli, consistent with the sensory profile of ASD (Horder et al., 2014) Immediately after responding to the cross on the critical trial, participants were asked to report their awareness of another stimulus presented on the screen and whether they had expected the stimulus beforehand (those reporting expectation beforehand were excluded), they were also asked to report how confident they were in their judgment (thus providing a measure of meta-cognitive awareness; Michel, 2023). If they did report detecting the stimulus, there were also asked to report its location from a list of four options. After an additional three line judgment trials, the stimulus and all awareness questions were presented a second time in a 'divided attention' trial where some expectation of the stimulus was expected. After another filler line judgment trial, participants completed a 'full attention' trial where they told to ignore the cross and search for the additional shape on the screen and report their awareness. Participants who reported not seeing the stimulus on this trial were excluded.

In a second pre-registered version of the task run only in Sample 8, participants completed more detailed awareness checks to ensure that they had not misunderstood task instructions, being asked to report on the features of the unexpected stimulus from a list of four options (see Supplementary materials 3 for further details).

Classification of Inattentional Blindness.

There is substantial variation across inattentional blindness studies in how 'detected' versus 'missed' outcomes are defined. A key source of inconsistency is the treatment of subjectively-reported detection: some studies classify subjective detection alone as 'detected' (Lee & Telch, 2008). In contrast, other studies place participants who report subjective awareness into the 'missed' category if they cannot provide accurate feature or location information (Kreitz et al., 2015), while others exclude these 'subjective-detection-without-identification' cases from analysis altogether (Bredemeier & Simons, 2012).

The present study adopted a stricter criterion, requiring participants to both subjectively-detect and accurately locate the stimulus to be allocated to the 'detected' category. Only participants who reported not detecting any unexpected stimulus were categorized as 'missed'. Based on neural evidence that low-level detection of stimulus (without stimulus identification) still elicits distinct neural activity, relative to an undetected stimulus (Koivisto et al., 2017; Wiens et al., 2023), we excluded participants who subjectively detected but mislocated the stimulus from either group in our primary analysis. However, this 'subjective detection only' group was examined in further exploratory analyses.

Demographic Questions

All participants were asked to report their age in an open response box.

Participants were asked to report the gender they identified as from the following options: 'female', 'male', 'different gender', 'prefer not to say'. No other demographic measures were included.

Additional Measures

In samples 3 and 4 a demonstration version of a letter identification task, not calibrated for the experimental setting, was also included for educational purposes in the undergraduate research methods workshop. Sample 7 also included the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (Marks, 1973), which was collected as part of a separate investigation (Cabbai et al., unpublished); and an in-house scale measuring the frequency of negative real-world outcomes, however, most participants reported zero on this scale, preventing analysis of this data. As mentioned above, sample 8 was collected for the purpose of a separate study and included several other questionnaires relating to that study's aims (http://osf.io/3hqu7). However, only the OAQ and IB data from that dataset was accessed by the first author of the present investigation.

Transparency and Openness

We have reported how we determined our sample sizes, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures collected in the study including those not analysed. All data, analysis code, and research materials which are not already freely accessible are available via the Open Science Framework (OSF), link: https://osf.io/hg4us/?view_only=e333f288e42c443497fe764238cad566. Data were analysed using R-Studio software (R-Studio Team, 2020), all specific packages utilised for these analyses are listed next to the relevant analysis. Sample 8 was preregistered via the OSF: https://osf.io/3je7y.

Results

OAQ Factor Structure

Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA)

After an initial four-factor structure was identified through EFA in Sample 3 (see Supplementary materials 4 for full details), we conducted CFA with maximum likelihood estimation to test the best fitting theoretical model to the data, in Samples 4 and 5 which were adequately sized to test the models. Responses of the few individuals who had participated in both Samples 4 and 5 were excluded from the CFA in Sample 5 to maintain independence of data. The CFA was then replicated on our pre-registered sample (Sample 8). This revealed that a bi-factor model was the best fitting and most plausible (see Table 2; Figure 2; See Supplementary materials 6 for full CFA analysis). Within the bi-factor model, most items reflect a common general Observant Attention factor, with three contributing factors consisting of Noticing, Alerting, and Olfactory awareness (see Table 3). Within the model, the fourth Distractibility factor was modelled as a distinct factor not contributing to the general factor, as it reflects difficulty sustaining attention on a primary task rather than awareness of external stimuli. Consistent with this, there was only a modest relationship between these factors across samples (i.e., r ≤ ±.19; see Supplementary materials 7 for individual subscales).

The global fit indices revealed that the bi-factor model was a good fit to the data, for Sample 4: χ 2 (136) = 284.54, p < .001, CFI = .92, RMSEA = .05, 90CI[.05, .06], SRMR = .05, Sample 5: χ 2 (136) = 257.70, p < .001, CFI = .91, RMSEA = .06, 90CI[.05, .07], SRMR = .06; and the finalized 19-item version in Sample 8: χ 2 (136) = 289.34, p < .001, CFI = .93, RMSEA = .05, 90CI[.05, .06], SRMR = .06.

Further, nested-model comparisons showed that the bi-factor model was a significantly better fit than the four-factor model in both Sample 4, Δχ 2 (10) = 27.80, p = .002; Sample 5, Δχ 2 (10) = 38.14, p < .001; and Sample 8 data: Δχ 2 (10) = 60.54, p < .001.

Additionally, retrospective analysis of the bi-factor model in Sample 2 revealed a good fit to the data, χ 2 (136) = 222.83, p < .001, CFI = .95, RMSEA = .04, 90CI[.03, .05], SRMR = .05, and that this was also a significantly better fit to the data relative to a four-factor model, Δχ 2 (10) = 41.35, p < .001.

Therefore, the CFA suggests that Observant Attention consistently and reliably reflects a general factor, supporting the computation of a general Observant Attention score along with use of specific subscales.

Interpretation of Factor Structure and Subscales

Although the focus of our investigation was on establishing an overall Observant Attention measure, given the replicability of the factor structure we have also included consideration of the factors as subscales in all analyses to follow. See Table 3 for broad summary of the contents of each subscale and relationships with other attentional measures. Of the three Observant Attention subscales, the first ('Noticing awareness') was based on the first factor extracted in our EFA. As can be seen in Table 2, the items in this subscale tend to reflect the awareness of unexpected but benign visual stimuli in the environment or the general ability to be observant of the surroundings. Interestingly, despite deliberately generating additional items across different senses that would plausibly load on this factor during our item refinement process (see Supplementary Materials 4), the items within this factor reflected predominantly detection of visual stimuli or visual memory ability.

The second Observant Attention subscale ('Alerting awareness') based on the second factor to emerge in the EFA, consisted of items referring to the detection and shifting of attention to a new unanticipated stimulus, when previously focused on something else. The stimuli referred to in these items were all motivationally relevant and required an immediate response, either due to presenting a threat or relevance to a current goal. Unlike the Noticing awareness factor, these items referred to stimuli across multiple senses (i.e., visual, auditory, tactile).

Table 3. Descriptions of each Observant Attention questionnaire subscale, and convergent and divergent constructs.

The final Observant Attention subscale ('Olfactory awareness') was the fourth to emerge in the EFA and consisted of items referring to the detection of unanticipated smells. This two-item factor referred to both neutral 'novel' smells and unpleasant smells, suggesting a general olfactory ability rather than a purely affective or motivational response.

The final subscale ('Distractibility') was based on the third factor to emerge in the EFA. This subscale, which does not contribute to the overall Observant Attention score, was composed of items reflecting the ability to voluntarily focus attention and ignore distraction.

Internal Reliability Analysis

Internal reliability was assessed using McDonald's omega total (ωt) omega which accounts for the factor structure across items alongside a general factor in a bi-factor solution; though the total scale and subscales were also analysed using Cronbach's alpha, with the exception of the two-item Olfactory awareness subscale

All analyses were computed using the psych package for R (Revelle, 2008; see Table 4, and Supplementary materials 7 for full details).

The computation of the ωt for the overall Observant Attention scale was computed by allowing all items to load on the general factor, excluding items from the Distractibility subscale. This therefore allowed us to examine internal reliability by determining the proportion of variance in items attributable to all factors including a general factor. This revealed good to excellent reliability across samples (ωt > .87). For computation of ωt for the independent Observant Attention subscales, items from all four subscales were analysed and allowed to load on a general factor.

Across all large samples (i.e., Samples 2, 3, 4, 5, 8) ωt ranged from .75 to .86, suggesting good reliability. Consistent with the assessment of the bi-factor model using CFA, examination of the loadings on the general factor suggested that the Distractibility factor was unrelated to the general Observant Attention factor, as loadings of the Distractibility items were consistently the lowest across all samples, and often below .3.

Test-Retest Reliability

To assess the stability of the Observant Attention trait we conducted a testretest analysis in participants who completed the OAQ as part of both Sample 4 and 5. Participants in Sample 4 were asked whether they consented to be contacted at a later date via their email, which they provided. Participants were then contacted approximately a year later, asking whether they consented to participate in the To measure test-retest reliability, absolute agreement Intraclass Correlations (ICC) with 95% confidence intervals were computed with the T1 and T2 OAQ scores, though Pearson's r correlation coefficient was also reported for the relationship (see Table 5). Both were computed using the R psych package (Revelle, 2008). Across both the total Observant Attention score, and all subscales of the OAQ, there was a strong significant correlation between T1 and T2 reports. In comparison to established guidelines for interpreting ICC (Koo & Li, 2016), the total Observant Attention score as well as Noticing awareness and Olfactory awareness subscales demonstrated good test-retest reliability (ICC = .75 -.9), and the Alerting awareness and Distractibility subscales demonstrated moderate test-retest reliability (ICC = .5 -.75).

Distribution of Observant Attention

Having established the reliability of our measure, we next examined the distribution of the finalised Observant Attention total score across samples 2-8 made up of 2,185 unique participant responses. Across samples, the mean score was consistently slightly above the mid-point of the scale, reflecting a view of observant behaviour as being somewhat typical, with responses recorded across the full range of the scale (see Supplementary materials 7).

Gender Differences.

We compared the average total Observant Attention score, and OAQ subscale scores, between male (N = 663) and female (N = 1,502) participants (see Table 6). This was analysed using a linear mixed-effects randomintercept 'mega-analysis' approach, which pools across all individual participants' data whilst controlling for independent samples as a random effects factor. Due to the exploratory nature of these five contrasts, a Bonferroni adjusted criterion was applied ( = .01), meaning that 99% confidence intervals were computed for this analysis. To mitigate the effect of unbalanced group sizes, confidence intervals were bootstrapped with 1000 iterations. See Supplementary materials 8 for full details and analysis. All mega-analyses reported were computed using the lme4 and emmeans R packages (Bates et al., 2015; Lenth, 2024).

This exploratory comparison revealed that cumulatively there were significant differences reflecting higher scores on female versus male participants on the Noticing subscale, as well as the Olfactory subscale -this trend was reversed for the alerting scale where males scored higher, although the latter difference did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. The distractibility subscale also showed a significant difference, with female participants reporting higher distractibility. There were no significant gender differences on any other OAQ scores.

Relationship with Established Attentional Traits

To assess the cumulative evidence for the relationships with other plausibly related and distinct attentional constructs across samples, we analysed the zero order correlations between the total Observant Attention score, OAQ subscales, and established measures of attention. When a measure was taken from multiple samples, the cumulative correlation coefficient was computed using a linear mixedeffects random-intercept analysis, pooling across all participants with Sample as a random effects factor.

As can be seen in Table 7, the overall Observant Attention score showed no significant correlation with other established measures of attention, beyond a weak negative relationship with S-MW. We note that correlations with ACS and CFQ were estimated from a relatively small sample (n = 61). Consequently, we cannot rule out the possibility that relationships with these constructs would emerge in larger samples. However, we note that even these smaller samples were highly powered (1-β = .99) to detect statistically significant correlations where the true underlying effect size was r = .50 or greater, as would be expected if the overall Observant Attention factor were largely indexing the same underlying construct as these established measures. Hence, the trait variation captured by our Observant Attention measure does not appear to substantially overlap with that indexed by existing attentional trait measures.

The pattern of relationships observed across the OAQ subscales was also consistent with this interpretation (see Table 7). Distractibility was significantly related to all established attentional trait measures (which were also all significantly intercorrelated with each other; see Table 7, lower half), with most correlations in the moderate-to-strong range. By contrast, the three Observant Attention subscales collectively showed only five significant correlations across 24 comparisons, all of which were modest in magnitude. This contrasting pattern echoes the bifactor structure identified in the CFA, in which Distractibility emerged as a factor distinct from the general Observant Attention factor. Taken together, these findings are consistent with the view that, whereas Distractibility substantially overlaps with existing attentional traits, Observant Attention reflects a distinct attentional phenomenon.

Relationship with Neurodiversity

We next examined the relationship of the Observant Attention total score to trait differences linked to neurodiversity. Self-reported childhood ADHD symptoms were modestly inversely related to the overall Observant Attention score, as well as all the specific subscales of the OAQ. Distractibility, on the other hand, showed a moderate positive correlation with ADHD symptoms. As can be seen in Table 6, almost all Observant Attention subscales were significantly correlated with both lower inattentive and hyperactive impulsive symptoms.

A follow-up partial correlation analysis also confirmed that the Observant Attention total score correlated with ADHD symptoms independent of the Distractibility subscale, Sample 3: rpartial = -.26, p < .001; Sample 4: rpartial = -.18, p < .001, further suggesting an independent mechanism from attentional failures/control.

As can be seen in Table 8, the attention to detail subscale of the AQ showed a modest, yet significant, positive correlation with the total Observant Attention score as well as the Noticing and Alerting awareness subscales of the OAQ when computed cumulatively across samples using a mega-analysis approach. To assess whether there was a broader link between autistic traits and Observant Attention, we also analysed the correlation between responses from an associated dataset which was completed by 56 participants from Sample 5, containing responses on the full AQ, and the GSQ which assesses atypical sensory processing linked to ASD. This revealed that, in contrast to the pattern seen in relation to attention to detail, the total Observant Attention score was inversely correlated with most other autistic traits.

However, no overall significant negative relationship was found between the OAQ and AQ total score, likely due to the unique opposing positive correlation with attention to detail combined with the small sample only powered to detect a moderate correlation (minimum r = .4).

In terms of sensory experiences, the GSQ was negatively correlated with the total Observant Attention score, with the Alerting subscale being the primary significant negative predictor of this. Thus, it appears that Alerting is associated with reduced profile of abnormal sensory experiences of reduced hyposensitivity and hypersensitivity -often linked to ASD.

Relationship with Inattentional Blindness (IB)

We tested whether scores on our new measure, in terms of both the overall Observant Attention score and OAQ subscale scores, would differ as a function of both performance on an IB measure, and confidence in performance. As is standard for IB tasks, this analysis excluded participants who reported that they had expected the unexpected stimulus to appear on the critical trial We also excluded participants that were unable to detect the critical stimulus even when instructed to attend it on the full attention trial (for similar practice in studies of inter-individual differences in IB see Horwood & Beanland, 2016; Kreitz et al., 2015). The paired group comparisons were computed using a linear mixed-effects random-intercept 'mega-analysis' approach, pooling across individual participant data whilst including independent samples as a random effects factor. To mitigate the effect of unbalanced group sizes within the nest model, 95% confidence intervals were bootstrapped with 1000 iterations. The full analysis and results are reported in Supplementary materials 3.

Individuals who reported missing the unexpected stimulus (total N = 167 had significantly lower Noticing scores relative to those detected (total N = 274), Mdiff = .21, p = .028, 95CI[.03, .40], d = .23. Total Observant Attention Score was numerically lower among the missed versus detected group, but this difference was not statistically reliable (Mdiff = .13, p = .072, 95CI[-.01, .28], d = .18. No other Observant Attention subcale significantly predicted detection on the IB tas (ps > .13).

We also noted that an unexpectedly high proportion of the sample reported detection but mislocated the stimulus (total N = 397). Relative to the 'miss' group, this 'subjective-detection only' group also had higher Noticing scores, Mdiff = .24, p = .002, 95CI[.08, .41], d = .26, and higher overall Observant Attention score, Mdiff = .16, p = .012, 95CI[.04, .29], d = .22. The high proportion of participants who reported detecting the stimulus but were unable to locate it raised concerns as to whether participants were misunderstanding task instructions. This was addressed in our preregistered sample using a version of the task with more detailed awareness checks.

Here, a simpler linear model analysis with planned contrasts was used due to the single sample. This revealed no significant difference between those who detected Within this sample, the subjective-detection only group now reflected a much smaller proportion of the sample (n = 47), and showed a pattern in the opposing direction to the mega-analysis: Relative to those who missed the stimulus, this group reported lower overall Observant Attention, Mdiff = -.27, p = .029, 95CI[-.53, -.04], d = -.10, and Alerting awareness, Mdiff = -.47, p = .004, 95CI[-.84, -.12], d = -.13. More detailed analysis dividing the participants who detected the stimulus into those that could identify the stimulus features (n = 32) to those that couldn't (n = 94) revealed no significant differences, d ≤ ±.09, p ≥ .137.

Confidence Ratings

Assessing the mega-analytic correlations between OAQ scores and detection confidence revealed no significant relationships across any of the IB groups in the mega-analysis, r ≤ ±.07, p ≥ .412. (see Supplementary materials 3 for full details).

Similarly, in the pre-registered detailed awareness version, no correlations between OAQ and confidence ratings were significant, r ≤ ±.24, p ≥ .110.

Other Attentional Traits' Relation to IB

Although not the focus of the present project, for the interested reader

Supplement 3 presents the relationship between IB and other eight questionnaires administered in combination with the IB task as part of our data collection (Ns from 43 -294). No significant relationships were found, with the exception of a pattern involving CFQ which was based on a small sample (N = 43, with only 3 participants missing the stimulus), and hence of questionable reliability (see Simons et al., 2024).

Discussion

The present data provides the first empirical support for the 'Observant Attention Trait' -reflecting the general tendency to be observant. In a large-scale investigation, consisting of 2,441 responses from 8 separate samples, that were recruited over 8 years, we developed a highly reliable and replicable measure of this novel trait. A test-retest analysis revealed strong correlations between T1 and T2 reports (i.e., ICC = .81; r = .69), even after a delay of between 11 -15 months. The test-retest reliability of our measure is comparable to that associated with genetically determined stable attentional traits such as ADHD symptoms (Kessler et al., 2007; Matza et al., 2011; Silverstein et al., 2018). The reliability and stability of our measure hence supports the view of Observant Attention as a stable trait which varies across individuals, consistent with its use in popular culture.

Distinctiveness from Existing Attentional Traits

Importantly, our measure of Observant Attention did not substantially overlap with any existing attentional questionnaire measures. In the light of the high reliability of all measures concerned, it is striking that the total Observant Attention score measured by the OAQ showed little relationship to other attentional measures (all rs < .22), including attentional control, cognitive failures, hyperfocus, daydreaming, and mind-wandering; with the only statistically reliable correlation being a weak relationship with mind-wandering. This supports the view of Observant Attention as a distinct phenomenon from those indexed by these existing measures of attention.

The view of Observant Attention as a novel trait, relative to existing traits, is also echoed by our measure's internal factor structure (replicated across three samples, one pre-registered): Items indexing Observant Attention were consistently separated from those indexing focused attention/distractibility. Across samples, items constituting the Observant Attention factor were only weakly and negatively correlated with the distinct Distractibility subscale of the OAQ (k = 7, N = 2,185, r = -.20, 95CI[-.23, -.15]; see Supplementary materials 7 for full analysis). In contrast to the Observant Attention subscales, the Distractibility subscale showed moderate to strong correlations with existing attention measures. This is intriguing, and suggests that Observant Attention may be driven by different underlying mechanisms than the other attentional mechanisms, which have been predominantly linked to the latent variable of attentional control (e.g. Burgoyne & Engle, 2020; Unsworth & McMillan, 2014; Unsworth, Robison & Miller., 2021). Our newly established measure provides a tool for future research to test this possibility.

Links to Inattentional Blindness

Arguably the existing construct with greatest conceptual relevance to Observant Attention is not a trait measure but the phenomenon of inattentional blindness (IB). The present findings are broadly consistent with the empirical picture emerging from Simons et al.'s (2024; 2026) meta-analysis and large sample investigation, which indicated relatively limited associations between individual-difference measures and IB: In our mega-analysis (total N = 838), both total Observant Attention scores and the noticing subscale were higher among individuals who reported detecting the unexpected stimulus, but this effect was modest and reached significance only for the noticing subscale (Cohen's d = .23).

Likewise, we observed no reliable relationship within our smaller preregistered sample, which was powered to detect effects of d ≥ .29.

On one hand, the weakness and inconsistency of these associations could simply reflect the low reliability of single-trial tasks for assessing stable individual differences in attention. To our knowledge, all laboratory trait-attention measures that have been established as reliable involve averaging performance across multiple trials, and it is likely that considering only a single trial from any of these measures would substantially undermine their sensitivity. It is also possible that the specific IB paradigm used here taps into a somewhat different form of noticing from that measured by the OAQ. OAQ items primarily reference noticing stimuli that are meaningful or behaviorally relevant (e.g., socially or in terms of likely consequences), and that remain present for sustained periods, whereas our IB task featured a briefly presented, low-salience, meaningless stimulus. As presentation time, meaning, salience, and goal-relevance are known to modulate IB noticing rates, these differences might plausibly affect the underlying construct being measured (Horstmann & Ansorge, 2016; Koivisto & Revonsuo, 2007; Kreitz et al., 2016; Most et al., 2001).

Indeed, prior work has noted that weak cross-method correlations can sometimes occur when self-report and task measures of the same cognitive trait (e.g., executive function) in fact tap into different underlying constructs (e.g., everyday self-regulation and goal pursuit versus efficiency in tightly controlled tasks, Toplak et al., 2013; or different aspects of memory, Ralph et al., 2018). Hence, while divergence between self-report and task-based measures may partly reflect the low reliability of some cognitive tasks (Draheim et al., 2019; Hedge et al., 2018; Rouder et al., 2023), it should also be considered that laboratory tasks typically index a highly specific, constrained aspect of the construct, whereas questionnaires capture a wider range of real-world behaviors that may draw on partially distinct mechanisms.

On the other hand, IB paradigms undisputably measure noticing (or lack of), and there is robust meta-analytic evidence confirming the sensitivity of these paradigms to detect task-based effects on IB outcome (Hutchinson et al., 2022; Matias et al., 2022). It might reasonably be inferred, therefore, that any trait-related influences on IB may be likely to be smaller in magnitude than these situational effects, only becoming evident across large samples. Importantly, however, this does not imply that trait influences on noticing behavior are trivial: While an IB trial provides each participant with only one opportunity to notice an unexpected stimulus, real-world environments present an enormous number of noticing opportunities in any given day. A small effect that only emerges across unfeasibly large IB samples might therefore translate into meaningful, cumulative differences in everyday noticing.

As discussed in our introduction, enhanced Observant Attention could plausibly offer many real-world advantages across a wide range of contexts in which failures to notice important information can have negative, even disastrous, consequences (e.g., driving, police investigations, medical examinations). The OAQ could potentially play a complementary role to the IB paradigm in understanding real world noticing behavior -the latter lending itself to controlled experimental manipulations that allow the testing of causal hypotheses relating to situational influences on specific noticing outcomes, and the former providing a reliable and low-cost means of capturing trait influences (e.g., in longitudinal studies, testing whether OA predicts real-world outcomes over extended time-periods).

Potential Cognitive Underpinnings of Observant Attention

As noted in our introduction, the existing literature on individual differences in attention has identified attentional control (and in particular working memory capacity) as a key latent variable underlying a wide range of attention task performance differences. However, the lack of evidence in the present data for a substantive relationship between Observant Attention and other attentional traits linked to top-down attentional control makes it unlikely to be the primary driver of OA.

The notion that attentional control plays a lesser role in spontaneous noticing behaviour than other forms of attention (e.g., focused attention and distraction) is also consistent with the inattentional blindness literature: Recent meta-analyses found inconsistent results not only regarding the relationship of IB to working memory capacity (Simons et al., 2024), but also in the effects of experimental manipulations of working memory load on IB (Matias et al, 2022).

Established situational determinants of IB point to alternative candidates for mechanisms potentially underlying OA. For instance, it has been found that surprise and novelty of a stimulus reliably reduce the rates of IB (e.g., Horstmann & Ansorge, 2016), even for stimuli that aren't highly physically salient (Horstmann, 2015). It could be, therefore, that some individuals are more sensitive to, or attuned to, bottom-up signals from unexpected and novel stimuli.

Another potentially relevant factor implicated in noticing unexpected objects in IB research is perceptual capacity. When perceptual capacity is limited by task demands, the detection of irrelevant stimuli decreases (MacDonald & Lavie, 2008; 2011; Cartwright-Finch & Lavie, 2007; Forster & Spence, 2018), with a recent metaanalysis finding robust evidence for effects of perceptual task load on IB (Mattias, 2022). Outside of the IB literature, perceptual capacity has also been found to be subject to individual differences, for example, linked to age (Maylor & Lavie, 1998; Huang Pollck, Carr & Nigg, 2002) or video gaming experience (Green & Bavelier, 2003). Eayrs & Lavie (2018) established a subitizing task as a measure of individual differences in perceptual capacity, which predicted awareness in several tasks involving detection of expected stimuli (change blindness, load-induced blindness).

An interesting question is whether perceptual capacity differences might therefore also predict awareness of unexpected stimuli -our new measure could be used to explore this possibility.

It also appears worthwhile to consider the relationship between Observant attention and a wider range of perceptual traits. Our finding of a negative correlation between the OA and the Glasgow Sensory Questionnaire was perhaps surprising, and inconsistent with a role of sensory sensitivity in driving OA. However, it appears plausible that other perceptual differences might play a role. Across a battery of measures of attention and perception, Andermane et al., (2019), found that tasks which reflected the ability to maintain a stable and precise representation of visual stimuli in mind (e.g., binocular rivalry, visual short-term memory) loaded on a separate factor to those reflecting sensitivity to early visual perceptual input (e.g., contrast sensitivity, iconic memory). Interestingly, within the factor analysis, change blindness loaded on the first factor reflecting stability of mental representation, rather than the second visual sensitivity factor. Thus, the ability to mentally represent the external environment accurately may be required to notice subtle changes, and therefore might also plausibly be linked to observant attention.

Facets of Observant Attention

The main aim of this investigation was to identify a single Observant Attention trait. In keeping with this aim, across samples, CFA revealed that Observant Attention likely reflects a bi-factor structure, whereby items fall across a general Observant Attention factor, which can be computed as a total score. This general factor appeared to reflect the detection of stimuli varying in different intensities and across contexts, ranging from subtle features in the environment to salient motivationally relevant stimuli requiring a response. However, whilst the bi-factor model supported the calculation of a general Observant Attention score, it also consisted of multiple independent domain-specific factors which relate to specific aspects of Observant Attention, which could be computed as subscales. These were factors reflecting Noticing awareness, Alerting awareness, and Olfactory awareness.

We also found a Distractibility subscale, which was distinct from other Observant Attention factors, and reflects the inability to focus attention on a current target or goal.

Interestingly, the different Observant Attention subscales appeared to comprise different elements of perception and attention, and were differentially associated with other attentional measures. The three key features which differed between the subscales appeared to be the physical salience of the stimulus being observed, the current motivational relevance of the stimulus, and the sensory modality the stimulus was being observed in (see Table 3 for summary). These could point towards partially distinct underlying mechanisms or different levels of processing depending on sensory inputs or intensity. Indeed, evidence has shown visual dominance in perceptual processing, with other senses processed more intermittently, especially olfactory stimuli (Sinnett et al., 2007; Sela & Sobel, 2010).

Links to Neurodivergent Traits

Neurodivergent traits including ADHD and ASD symptoms have been linked to different perceptual and cognitive profiles, which could plausibly be correlated with greater Observant Attention (Grossman et al., 2015; Baron-Cohen, Scott et al., 2009).

Regarding ADHD, however, we found that reported childhood symptoms were inversely related to the total Observant Attention score for both hyperactiveimpulsive and inattentive symptoms. Across the subscales which contributed to the Observant Attention score, the strongest relationship with ADHD symptom scores was with the Alerting subscale. In contrast to the Observant Attention total score and subscales, the Distractibility subscale showed a strong positive relationship with ADHD symptoms, replicating previous evidence of the link between ADHD symptoms and behavioural measures of distractibility (Forster & Lavie, 2016).

Importantly, a partial correlation analysis confirmed that the Observant Attention total score was related to ADHD independent of Distractibility.

Such a result raises the interesting question of whether lower trait Observant Attention might contribute to the increased risk of negative life events seen in ADHD (Garcia et al., 2012). For example, reduced awareness, particularly in relation to 'alerting', might plausibility contribute to the increased risk of driving accidents seen in relation to both ADHD diagnosis and higher levels of trait ADHD symptoms (Vaa et al., 2014). Initial support for this notion can be found in the present paper's finding of a mediating role for Observant Attention, but not Distractibility, in the relationship between ADHD symptoms and poorer awareness of interpersonal distance -which may lead to unwanted social or public health costs from uncontrolled proximity to others (see Brown & Forster, 2023).

For ASD symptoms on the other hand, we found a more complex relationship across AQ and GSQ measures. Our primary focus within the investigation was the relationship between Observant Attention and the attention to detail subscale of the AQ, which exhibited a consistent positive relationship, in line with prior work showing a perceptual advantage in ASD (Constable et al., 2020; Remington et al., 2012). We, however, also found that across the remaining subscales of the AQ there was either no significant relationship or a significant negative relationship with Observant Attention. Similarly, the GSQ, which measures sensory sensitivity linked to ASD, was also significantly negatively correlated with Observant Attention. We note, however, that whereas the Attention to Detail findings were based on a substantially larger cumulative sample (N = 179), the broader AQ and GSQ analyses were based on a smaller sample (N = 56), and therefore the magnitude of these latter relationships should be interpreted with caution until replicated in larger samples. This preliminary evidence suggests a mixed picture in which trait Observant Attention is positively associated with attention to detail specifically, but may be negatively associated with other facets of ASD.

Limitations

The most obvious potential limitation of our measure is its subjective nature.

Our data provide convincing evidence that the extent to which people self-identify as being observant -in terms of whether they tend to spontaneously notice, or conversely overlook, information in their environment -is a stable trait. Given the absence of any reliable objective index of Observant Attention, it is not yet possible to verify the accuracy of these self-reports. However, existing evidence provides reassurance that humans can provide meaningful self-reports regarding cognitive phenomena: For example, self-reports of existing attentional traits (e.g., cognitive failures, inattention/distractibility), as well as other subjective phenomena (e.g., mind wandering), have been corroborated through objective structural and functional neural correlates (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2011; Geurts et al., 2013; Kanai et al., 2011; Hoogman et al., 2012; Sandberg et al., 2014). It therefore seems reasonable to expect that people could similarly self-report their Observant Attention.

We note that the wording of our items was designed to pick up on common sources of evidence regarding noticing tendencies, minimizing the need for metacognitive awareness (and, importantly, avoiding the oxymoronic requirement for 'awareness of awareness failures'). Reverse-coded items were intentionally constructed around situations in which failures of noticing are revealed through immediate consequences, feedback from others, or delayed realization (e.g., a driver honking to indicate a missed green light; a friend commenting on an unnoticed change; eventually becoming aware of persistent knocking). Indeed, when noticing lapses are revealed, they are often striking and memorable: The experience of discovering a failure of awareness can be emotionally salient or surprising, a phenomenon long noted in the inattentional blindness literature (e.g., Mack & Rock, 1998; Simons & Chabris, 1999), where participants frequently express shock at having missed an obvious event. As such, it appears plausible that these memorable feedback moments help individuals form stable impressions of their own noticing tendencies, without the need for introspective access.

Perhaps it might be argued that items measuring noticing successes (e.g., 'Always notice aesthetic details of rooms that I am in') are more reliant on metacognitive awareness. However, the fact that items measuring noticing successes and failures intercorrelate and load together on a single OA factor appears inconsistent with a driving role of meta-awareness in OA reports. In addition, we directly tested the association between OA and awareness confidence ratings, which are an established measure of meta-awareness of noticing and detection used in consciousness research (Fleming, 2024; Michel, 2023), including inattentional blindness judgments (Nartker et al., 2025; Pitts et al., 2012; Schelonka et al., 2017; Shafto & Pitts; 2015). Neither the mega-analysis nor the preregistered dataset showed any correlation.

A key question is, if our questionnaire were measuring something other than

Observant Attention, what could it be measuring? The limited overlap with measures such as the Cognitive Failures Questionnaire makes it unlikely that scores simply reflect a general tendency to acknowledge cognitive errors or, conversely, to view one's abilities positively. It is difficult to conceive of any alternative account in which a variable orthogonal to true OA would produce the observed pattern of responding.

In the absence of any plausible alternative account, the most parsimonious interpretation of our data is that our questionnaire simply measures what it appears to be measuring (as confirmed by both human raters and LLM analysis): The novel trait of Observant Attention.

Regarding validity, for now we conclude that our novel measure demonstrates strong reliability, content validity, and construct validity, as evidenced by its coherent factor structure and its discriminant relations with existing attentional trait measures.

Although laboratory tasks cannot provide a suitable criterion validity check for spontaneous noticing tendencies (as discussed above), there are other potential avenues for longer-term criterion validation. One is to examine predictive validity in longitudinal settings, where noticing successes and failures accumulate over many spontaneous noticing opportunities and potentially influence real-world outcomes (e.g., workplace or driving-related errors). Additional validity can also be established by identifying objective structural or functional neural correlates of OA, or to assess the heritability of OA traits -approaches that have been successfully applied to other cognitive constructs (Blokland et al., 2011; Geurts et al., 2013; Kanai et al., 2011; Hoogman et al., 2012). Another widely used method to validate self-report trait measures, is assessing the convergence between self-ratings and external informant ratings, which have been used to validate ADHD measures and diagnoses (Murphy & Schachar, 2000; Connolly et al., 2007). Work applying this approach to the OAQ is currently in progress in our lab.

The current investigation's aim was primarily to test for the novel trait of Observant Attention, introduce a reliable measure of this trait, and assess its relation to other attentional traits. We did not, however, test the widely held assumption that Observant Attention is a beneficial trait. It would, therefore, be interesting to explore trait Observant Attention's positive influence on the trajectory of people's lives, and its role in predicting factors such as academic, social, or occupational performance and success. Indeed, it could shape individuals' goals and behaviours, including selection of career paths or preferred environments.

Constraints on Generality

The main aim of the current investigation was to develop a novel measure of observant attention. This required multiple large samples for exploratory and confirmatory scale development stages. For this to be feasible in a manageable timeframe, we utilized the readily available undergraduate participant pools and large undergraduate workshop samples. We therefore acknowledge that the current samples were lacking diversity in age and level of education, and from a 'WEIRD' (Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic) society which only make up 12% of the global population (see Henrich et al., 2010). Whilst the homogeneous samples limit the generalizability of findings, the cost-effectiveness of the novel questionnaire tool can now facilitate future extensions across more varied samples. Indeed, we found evidence of gender differences, suggesting evidence of demographic variation.

Conclusion

Awareness of unexpected external events has previously been assumed to be mostly determined by situational factors rather than trait tendencies, largely based on research using the IB paradigm. Our novel self-report measure challenges this assumption by providing evidence for a stable Observant Attention trait, reflecting the extent to which individuals report habitually noticing even subtle differences in the environment, or conversely missing even obvious stimuli. Interestingly, despite high reliability of all measures concerned, this trait was only modestly related to other well established attention traits. The measure introduced here represents a tool that allows for the first time the systematic exploration of this trait, including its objective correlates, underlying mechanisms, and how it shapes our lives.

The total GSQ score within Sample 5 was linked to the current data from a separate investigation after mean score was computed, preventing reliability analysis across the individual items.Static Inattentional Blindness Task(Newby & Rock, 1998) In Samples 2, 5, 6 and 7 participants completed a single ten trial sequence on a static IB task taken from Newby & Rock (1998; see Figure1, and Supplementary Materials 3 for specific details). The task required to identify the longest arm of a central cross stimulus. After three trials of the cross-judgment task, an unexpected critical stimulus was presented in the periphery of the screen next to the cross. The critical stimulus was a .9° x .9° grey square (RGB: 120,120,120) presented randomly in either the top-left, top-right, bottom-left, or bottom-right quadrant of the cross, 5.2° from the centre of the screen. The outcome variable was whether they perceived an unexpected critical stimulus.
